title: Domains: true parallelism in OCaml 5
body: Before OCaml 5 a single runtime lock meant only one thread could run OCaml code at a time. A *domain* is a unit of real parallelism: `Domain.spawn f` starts `f` on another core, and `Domain.join d` waits for it and returns its result (re-raising its exception). Each domain has its own minor heap, so allocation does not contend.

Divide work so domains share nothing mutable. Splitting an array into disjoint ranges, letting each domain return a partial sum, and combining the results on the main domain needs no locks at all. Spawning is not free, so create about `Domain.recommended_domain_count ()` domains at most and give each a substantial chunk.

Check the edges. An empty array, fewer elements than domains and a length that does not divide evenly are where chunking code breaks. Write the range arithmetic carefully with `min n (d * size)` so the last chunk is short rather than out of bounds.
challenge: src/psum.ml returns 0. Implement `sum ~domains a` by splitting `a` into `domains` contiguous chunks (the last may be short or empty), summing each chunk in its own domain, joining them and adding the partial sums. Reject `domains < 1` with `Invalid_argument`.
projectInstructions: Run `dune test --root .`. The test checks uneven chunking, an empty array and more domains than elements. Edit only src/psum.ml.
question: Why can domains sum disjoint array ranges without a lock?
correct: They only read shared immutable data and each returns its own partial result, so nothing is written concurrently
wrong: OCaml locks every array access automatically
Domains run one at a time
reasoning: Data races need concurrent access with at least one write to the same location; disjoint reads and private results have none.
